name: Sulayhid Dynasty
description: The Sulayhid dynasty ruled an influential realm across the southern and central highlands of Yemen following its establishment by Ali al-Sulayhi. Operating in close religious and political alignment with the Cairo-based Fatimid Caliphate, the realm championed Ismaili Shi'ism while suppressing regional adversaries, particularly the Zaidis in the north. Under the revered queen regent Arwa al-Sulayhi, governance shifted southwards towards Jibla, ushering in an era of agricultural revival, urban development and maritime trade. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Sana'a; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Ismaili Shia Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Sulayhid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1047; Disestablished: 1138

name: Taifa of Lérida
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Lérida emerged as an autonomous Islamic principality in the north-eastern march of al-Andalus amidst the fragmentation of the Caliphate of Córdoba. Governed primarily by the Banu Hud dynasty, the border realm guarded the Segre river valley while contending with aggressive Christian expansionism from the County of Barcelona and neighbouring Aragon. Its emirs frequently balanced costly tribute payments to Christian counts against internecine conflicts with the rival Banu Hud rulers of Zaragoza until the eventual Almoravid conquest. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Lérida; Common languages: Andalusian Arabic, Mozarabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Hud; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1039; Disestablished: 1110

name: Normans
label: norse/viking polities;norman polities in southern italy
description: The Normans in southern Italy established an initial territorial confederation centred on the fortress town of Melfi following their victorious campaigns against Byzantine authority in Apulia. Functioning under the shared leadership of mercenary captains allied with the Lombard nobility, this nascent lordship consolidated control over the Vulture region through rapid fort construction and mobile cavalry warfare. It provided the essential institutional foundation from which the Hauteville family soon formalised an organised county across the Mezzogiorno. \n\n Status: Autonomous military confederation; Capital: Melfi; Common languages: Old Norman, Latin, Neapolitan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Military lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 17 March 1041; Disestablished: 1 October 1042; Succeeded by: County of Apulia and Calabria

name: Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate
description: The Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate arose when dynastic rivalries split the Karluk Turkic realm into two autonomous branches during the mid-eleventh century. Ruling across the Tarim Basin, Semirechye and parts of the Tian Shan range from royal centres at Balasagun and Kashgar, the Great Khagan governed according to traditional dual monarchy principles. The realm patronised Perso-Turkic Islamic letters and maintained lucrative Silk Road caravan commerce before succumbing to Seljuk overlordship in the early twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign khaganate; Capital: Balasagun; Common languages: Khaqani Turkic, Persian, Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Diarchy monarchy; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1042; Preceded by: Kara-Khanid Khanate; Succeeded by: Western Liao

name: Western Kara-Khanid Khanate
description: The Western Kara-Khanid Khanate formed following the formal partition of the greater Karluk empire, securing dominion over Transoxiana and the Fergana Valley. Governing from the ancient urban hub of Samarkand, the western khagans presided over an ethnically diverse population of Sogdian townsmen and nomadic Turkic pastoralists while embedding Perso-Islamic administrative traditions. Despite considerable architectural and scholarly patronage, domestic succession feuds progressively weakened the regime, leaving it vulnerable to imperial Seljuk subjugation by the century's end. \n\n Status: Sovereign khaganate; Capital: Samarkand; Common languages: Khaqani Turkic, Persian, Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Monarchy; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1042; Disestablished: 1096; Preceded by: Kara-Khanid Khanate

name: County of Apulia and Calabria
label: norse/viking polities;norman polities in southern italy
description: The County of Apulia and Calabria developed as an autonomous Norman state in southern Italy under the leadership of William Iron Arm of the Hauteville dynasty. Centred at the fortified hilltop town of Melfi, the county coordinated twelve Norman baronies to systematically wrest control of fertile lowlands from Byzantine catepans and neighbouring Lombard princes. Comital rule brought military organisation and feudal vassalage to the region before Duke Robert Guiscard received formal ducal investiture from the Papacy in 1059. \n\n Status: Feudal county; Capital: Melfi; Common languages: Old Norman, Latin, Calabrian, Neapolitan; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hauteville; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1042; Succeeded by: Duchy of Apulia and Calabria

name: Kingdom of Norway
description: The Kingdom of Norway entered into a dynastic personal union with Denmark during the reign of King Magnus the Good, who inherited the Danish crown following the demise of Harthacnut. Magnus governed his northern homeland through native lagmann assemblies and regional assemblies while directing military expeditions southwards to secure the Danish borders against Wendish incursions. The arrangement maintained Norwegian administrative customs and domestic laws until Magnus died in 1047, leading to a royal succession that restored an autonomous Norwegian monarchy under Harald Hardrada. \n\n Status: Kingdom in personal union; Administrative seat: Mobile court; Common languages: Old Norse; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Fairhair; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1043; Disestablished: 1048; Preceded by: Kingdom of Norway

name: Taifa of Lorca
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Lorca was an independent Andalusian emirate established in south-eastern Iberia when local governor Ma'n ibn Sumadih broke away from the authority of Valencia. Occupying a strategic highland bastion along the Guadalentín river, the small principality commanded vital trade and defensive routes between Murcia, Granada and the Mediterranean coast. Lorca maintained its sovereignty through pragmatic diplomacy and fortress architecture until surrounding regional powers and eventual Christian crusades brought about its incorporation into neighbouring Murcia. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Lorca; Common languages: Andalusian Arabic, Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1042; Disestablished: 1250; Succeeded by: Taifa of Murcia

name: Ziyarid Dynasty
label: iranian intermezzo
description: The Ziyarid dynasty functioned as a subordinate princely state along the southern Caspian littoral after Seljuk armies overran northern Iran in 1042. Confined largely to the rugged mountainous terrain of Tabaristan and Gorgan, the Daylamite rulers acknowledged Seljuk suzerainty and rendered tribute while retaining internal administrative autonomy over their forested redoubts. The princely court preserved rich Persian cultural traditions and fostered scholarly works until expanding Nizari Ismaili forces ultimately dismantled the last remnants of the dynasty around 1090. \n\n Status: Vassal principality; Capital: Amol; Common languages: Persian, Tabari, Gilaki; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Ziyarid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1043; Disestablished: 1091

name: Kingdom of Nri
description: The Kingdom of Nri flourished as a sacred ritual and political state across the northern and western reaches of Igboland in what is now south-eastern Nigeria. Governed by a divine priest-king titled the Eze Nri, the realm expanded its authority not through territorial military conquest but via moral diplomacy, spiritual purification, trade networks and the conferring of prestigious titled honours. Renowned for its sophisticated bronze metalworking found at Igbo-Ukwu, Nri served as an egalitarian sanctuary until British colonial pacification dissolved its monarchical prerogatives in the early twentieth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Igbo-Ukwu; Common languages: Igbo; Religion: Traditional Igbo religion; Government: Sacred monarchy; Ruler title: Eze Nri; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 1044; Disestablished: 1911

name: Commune of Forlimpopoli
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Forlimpopoli developed as a self-governing medieval city-state in the fertile Romagna plain along the ancient Via Emilia. Operating within the nominal framework of the Holy Roman Empire, the town established communal consuls, merchant guilds and civic courts to assert independence from neighbouring bishoprics and regional feudal magnates. Forlimpopoli relied on its agricultural wealth and fortified perimeter to navigate endemic regional conflicts between Guelph and Ghibelline factions until rival regional despots subjugated the municipality in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Self-governing city-state; Capital: Forlimpopoli; Common languages: Latin, Romagnol, early Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Communal republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1045; Disestablished: 1301; Historical region: Romagna

name: County of Toggenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Toggenburg was an imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire located across the Thur valley in modern eastern Switzerland. Ruled by the comital House of Toggenburg from their stronghold at Lichtensteig, the dynasty expanded its territorial influence through matrimonial alliances, imperial privileges and the strategic acquisition of Alpine transit routes. The county remained a powerful regional force in Swabian and Helvetian politics until the comital line died out in 1436, triggering the Old Zurich War over the contested inheritance. \n\n Status: Imperial county; Capital: Lichtensteig; Common languages: Alemannic German, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Toggenburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Late Middle Ages; Established: 1045; Disestablished: 1436

name: Kediri Kingdom
description: The Kediri Kingdom, historically recognised as Panjalu, was a major Hindu-Buddhist realm established in eastern Java following King Airlangga's partition of the Kahuripan domain. Centred along the fertile basin of the Brantas River at Dahanapura, the realm prospered through extensive maritime rice commerce, spice trading and vigorous royal patronage of Old Javanese classical literature. Kediri dominated inland and coastal trade routes until Ken Arok defeated the last monarch, Kertajaya, at the Battle of Ganter in 1222, establishing the Singhasari kingdom. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Daha; Common languages: Old Javanese, Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Maharaja; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1046; Disestablished: 1222; Succeeded by: Singhasari

name: Kingdom of Artsakh
description: The Kingdom of Artsakh was a medieval Armenian highland monarchy that maintained Christian autonomy across the mountainous provinces of Artsakh and Syunik following the decline of Bagratid Armenia. Governed by a branch of the ancient Aranshahik dynasty from fortified positions in the Khachen valley, the realm preserved Armenian political customs and religious autonomy amidst surrounding Turkish invasions. The rulers sustained independent mountain defences, monastic institutions and strategic diplomatic alliances until integrating more formally into the pan-Caucasian Christian alliance led by the Kingdom of Georgia in 1121. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Khachen; Common languages: Armenian; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Church; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Khachen; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1046; Disestablished: 12 August 1121

name: Kingdom of Janggala
description: The Kingdom of Janggala was a Hindu-Buddhist principality in eastern Java created through the partition of the Kahuripan realm by King Airlangga for his son. Based near the mouth of the Brantas river around present-day Surabaya, Janggala held extensive coastal ports that profited from lucrative spice routes connecting the Indonesian archipelago to mainland Asia. The kingdom engaged in protracted territorial rivalry with its western sibling state Panjalu until Jayabhaya of Kediri successfully conquered Janggala in 1137, reuniting the ancestral Javanese crown. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Surabaya; Common languages: Old Javanese, Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism, Buddhism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1046; Disestablished: 1137; Succeeded by: Kediri Kingdom

name: Kingdom of Syunik
description: The Kingdom of Syunik, frequently referred to as the Kingdom of Kapan, was an independent Armenian feudal monarchy situated in the rugged southeastern highlands of historical Armenia. Governed by the native Syunid dynasty from their fortified mountain citadel at Kapan, the kingdom outlasted many neighbouring Bagratid principalities through skilful exploitation of its formidable natural topography. Syunik preserved thriving Armenian monastic foundations and urban trade guilds until persistent Seljuk campaigns devastated the realm in the early twelfth century, ending its royal independence. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kapan; Common languages: Armenian; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Church; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Siunia dynasty; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1046; Disestablished: 1125

name: Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget
description: The Kingdom of Tashir-Dzoraget was an Armenian highland state ruled by the Kiurikian branch of the Bagratuni royal house across the borderlands of northern Armenia and southern Georgia. Operating from strongholds at Matsnaberd and the formidable canyon citadel of Lori Berd, the monarchs asserted sovereign independence following the fall of Ani to Byzantine forces. Tashir-Dzoraget defended critical mountain passes against regional nomadic incursions until Seljuk raids compelled its princes to yield territory and accept incorporation into the expanding Kingdom of Georgia. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Lori Berd; Common languages: Armenian; Religion: Armenian Apostolic Church; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kiurikian; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1046; Disestablished: 1119; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Prince-Bishopric of Toul
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Toul was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire located in the upper Moselle valley of Lorraine. Established as an imperial immediacy by the German emperors, the bishops exercised both temporal sovereignty over comital estates and spiritual authority across a broad diocesan domain. Toul maintained its autonomy amidst chronic territorial disputes with the dukes of Lorraine until 1552, when King Henry II of France occupied the city and established French royal administration over the Three Bishoprics. \n\n Status: Prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Toul; Common languages: Middle French, Latin, German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early Modern era; Established: 1049; Disestablished: 1553; Succeeded by: Three Bishoprics

name: Muslim State of Malta
description: The Muslim State of Malta was an autonomous insular polity that arose after Arab and Berber settlers rebuilt the ancient hilltop citadel of Melite, naming it Mdina. The settlement revitalised the Maltese archipelago through advanced cistern-based agriculture, cotton cultivation and Mediterranean maritime trade linked to Islamic Sicily and Ifriqiya. Operating as an independent community under local Muslim leadership, the island maintained self-government until Count Roger I of Sicily landed a Norman expedition in 1091, imposing tributary status on the Muslim garrison. \n\n Status: Sovereign insular emirate; Capital: Mdina; Common languages: Siculo-Arabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Oligarchic emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1050; Disestablished: 1 August 1091; Succeeded by: County of Sicily

name: Zirid Dynasty
label: berber kingdoms
description: The Zirid dynasty ruled an autonomous Sanhaja Berber emirate along the eastern Maghreb coastline of Ifriqiya following its definitive rupture with the Cairo-based Fatimids in the mid-eleventh century. After shifting their royal seat to the fortified port of Mahdia to escape devastating incursions by the nomadic Banu Hilal tribes, the Zirids focused on maritime commerce and naval defence across the central Mediterranean. Their naval dominance declined under persistent Norman raids from Sicily, ultimately culminating in the loss of their coastal strongholds to the Almohad Caliphate. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Mahdia; Common languages: Berber, Maghrebi Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zirid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1050; Disestablished: 1153; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: County of Geisenhausen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Geisenhausen was a small comital territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Kleine Vils valley in Lower Bavaria. Administered from the market settlement and castle of Geisenhausen, the comital line wielded local judicial rights, tolls and forest prerogatives amidst a network of imperial noble domains. The county maintained its autonomous status through shifting feudal allegiances until the expanding House of Wittelsbach absorbed its lands and rights into the Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut during the late fourteenth century. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Geisenhausen; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Late Middle Ages; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1394; Historical region: Bavaria

name: County of Mansfeld
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Mansfeld was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the eastern Harz foreland of modern Saxony-Anhalt. Possessing substantial silver and copper mining deposits around Eisleben and Mansfeld Castle, the comital house derived considerable financial wealth and political stature within the Saxon Circle. Despite multiple partitions among comital branches and devastating damage during the Thirty Years' War, Mansfeld preserved its imperial immediacy until accumulating debt prompted sovereign annexation by the Electorate of Saxony and Prussia. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Eisleben, Lutherstadt; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Lutheranism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Mansfeld; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early Modern era; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1781

name: Hondpa
description: Hondpa was an ancient princely estate established amidst the forested hills of modern Odisha in eastern India by Raja Pratap Deo of the Kadamba dynasty. Serving as the foundational territory of what subsequently became the Athmallik State, the principality commanded key agrarian clearings and tribal trade tracks near the Mahanadi River basin. Hondpa's rulers maintained autonomy through strategic tributary relations with regional empires while preserving native administrative customs, enduring for centuries prior to its administrative modernisation during the British Raj. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Hondpa; Common languages: Odia; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kadamba dynasty; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1875; Succeeded by: Athmallik State

name: Imperial City of Boppard
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial City of Boppard functioned as a self-ruling municipal commune of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the Rhine Gorge south of Koblenz. Deriving substantial revenues from river tolls, vineyard cultivation and merchant transport along the Rhine waterway, Boppard secured imperial immediacy directly from the German monarchs. The citizens guarded their civic liberties and urban privileges against territorial encroachers until Emperor Henry VII mortgaged the city to the Archbishopric of Trier in 1309, sparking fierce local resistance. \n\n Status: Free imperial city; Capital: Boppard; Common languages: Middle High German, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Urban commune; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1310; Succeeded by: Electorate of Trier

name: Jasrota State
description: Jasrota State was a Rajput hill kingdom situated across the sub-Himalayan Shivalik ranges between the Ravi and Ujh rivers in south-eastern Jammu. Established by Raja Jas Dev of the Dogra royal house, the kingdom was defended by seven prominent stone fortresses, canal networks and protected terraced valleys. Jasrota developed into a distinguished centre of Pahari miniature painting and temple architecture while preserving its independence from lowland sultanates until nineteenth-century expansionism under the Sikh Empire ended comital autonomy. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Jasrota; Common languages: Dogri, Takri, Urdu; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Dogra dynasty; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early Modern era; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1802

name: Kangra Kingdom
description: The Kangra Kingdom was an ancient Hindu monarchy located in the Western Himalayas across modern Himachal Pradesh, ruled by the illustrious Katoch dynasty. Centred around the formidable Kangra Fort overlooking the Banganga River, the state commanded lucrative pilgrimage routes and fertile Alpine valleys in the Punjab Hills. Kangra defended its sovereign authority against numerous external incursions by regional sultanates and the Mughal Empire, renowned for its patronage of distinct Kangra painting styles before nineteenth-century Sikh subjugation. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kangra; Common languages: Kangri, Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Katoch; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early Modern era; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1811; Succeeded by: Sikh Empire

name: Kumarsain State
description: Kumarsain State was a Himalayan hill principality established in the upper Satluj River valley of what is now the Shimla district in Himachal Pradesh. Founded in the eleventh century by an offshoot of the Katoch or Dogra nobility, the state controlled important mountain passes, terrace agriculture and early caravan routes linking northern Punjab with western Tibet. Its rulers exercised autonomous local governance and judicial authority through traditional village councils until broader regional conflicts reshuffled the political hierarchy of the Punjab Hill States. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Kumharsain; Common languages: Pahari, Hindi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Princely monarchy; Ruler title: Rana; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1451; Historical region: Punjab Hills

name: Manding Kingdom
description: The Manding Kingdom emerged as a unified Malinke polity across the upper Niger and Sankarani river basins following the triumph of the Keita Konate clan over rival regional lineages. Centred at Kangaba near the modern border of Mali and Guinea, the realm laid the institutional, cultural and military foundations that later blossomed into the vast Mali Empire under Sundiata Keita. Retaining sacred ancestral shrines and traditional chiefdom structures, Kangaba maintained continuous political and spiritual relevance as a sovereign Mandinka bastion across centuries. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Kangaba; Common languages: Mandinka, Malinke; Religion: Traditional African religion, Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Keita; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Modern era; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 2 October 1958

name: Signoria of Lavagna
label: holy roman empire
description: The Signoria of Lavagna was an autonomous feudal domain established along the eastern Ligurian coast around the mouth of the Entella River. Ruled by the Fieschi family, styled the Counts of Lavagna, the lordship held extensive castles, agricultural estates and maritime anchorages across the Riviera di Levante. The dynasty leveraged its strategic coastal position and papal connections to maintain autonomy from the burgeoning maritime Republic of Genoa until communal treaties gradually integrated the lordship into the Genoese state. \n\n Status: Feudal lordship; Capital: Lavagna; Common languages: Ligurian, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Dynastic lordship; Ruling dynasty: Fieschi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1051; Disestablished: 1199; Succeeded by: Republic of Genoa

name: Soomra Dynasty
description: The Soomra dynasty established a sovereign indigenous realm across Sindh in modern Pakistan after liberating the lower Indus Valley from Ghaznavid imperial dominance. Ruling initially from Mansura and subsequently from Thari, the dynasty adhered to Ismaili Shi'ism and acknowledged nominal caliphal ties with Cairo and Baghdad while fostering local Sindhi culture and commerce. The Soomras secured extensive agrarian canals and maritime trade through the Indus delta, preserving their independence for three centuries until internal discord enabled the rise of the Samma dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Mansura; Common languages: Sindhi, Arabic; Religion: Shia Ismaili Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Soomra; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1052; Disestablished: 1352; Succeeded by: Samma Dynasty

name: Uqaylid Dynasty
description: The Uqaylid dynasty operated as a prominent Shia Arab vassal principality during the second half of the eleventh century, centred upon the strategic Upper Mesopotamian city of Mosul. Following the Seljuk expansion into Iraq, the Uqaylid emirs accepted Seljuk suzerainty and contributed auxiliary cavalry while retaining extensive hereditary dominion across the Jazira and northern Syria. The dynasty governed a diverse population of Arabs, Kurds and Syriac Christians until dynastic rivalries and direct Seljuk imperial intervention ended Uqaylid comital rule in 1096. \n\n Status: Vassal emirate; Capital: Mosul; Common languages: Arabic, Syriac, Kurdish; Religion: Shia Islam; Government: Emirate; Ruling dynasty: Uqaylid; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1053; Disestablished: 1096; Overlord: Seljuk Empire

name: County of Brehna
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Brehna was an imperial comital domain of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the fertile lowlands between the Margraviate of Meissen and the Saxon marchlands. Centred at Brehna Castle southwest of Bitterfeld, the territory was ruled by an offshoot of the illustrious House of Wettin to consolidate Germanic control along the eastern Slavic frontiers. The counts oversaw agricultural development, fortress expansion and judicial administration across the gau until broader dynastic consolidations reshaped comital boundaries in the twelfth century. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Brene; Common languages: Middle High German, Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wettin; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1054; Disestablished: 1128

name: Emirate of Agrigento
label: sicilian taifas
description: The Emirate of Agrigento arose as an independent taifa in south-western Sicily following the fragmentation of the Kalbid Emirate of Palermo. Governed from the fortified heights of ancient Agrigento by local Arab and Berber military chieftains, the emirate controlled fertile grain plains and southern coastal ports along the Mediterranean. The regime became deeply embroiled in civil wars against rival Sicilian factions at Syracuse and Palermo, weakening its defensive posture just as Norman expeditions began their coordinated subjugation of the island. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Agrigento; Common languages: Siculo-Arabic, Byzantine Greek; Religion: Islam; Government: Military emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1054; Disestablished: 1066; Preceded by: Emirate of Sicily

name: Emirate of Catania
label: sicilian taifas
description: The Emirate of Catania was a short-lived breakaway Islamic principality established on the eastern coast of Sicily amidst the collapse of centralised Kalbid authority. Headquartered in the port city of Catania beneath the slopes of Mount Etna, the emirate derived wealth from maritime trade, fishing and irrigated citrus agriculture. Constrained by fierce territorial conflicts with rival emirs at Syracuse and Agrigento, Catania struggled to maintain independent sovereignty and was rapidly absorbed into neighbouring spheres of influence during the opening stages of the Norman invasion. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Catania; Common languages: Siculo-Arabic, Byzantine Greek; Religion: Islam; Government: Military emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1054; Disestablished: 1056; Preceded by: Emirate of Sicily

name: Emirate of Palermo
label: sicilian taifas
description: The Emirate of Palermo formed as an autonomous factional state in north-western Sicily when the breakdown of unified Kalbid rule fragmented the island into competing taifas. Centred at the cosmopolitan metropolis of Palermo, the emirate retained rich artisanal industries, extensive maritime commerce and sophisticated hydraulic garden irrigation networks. Despite its commercial pre-eminence and substantial defensive walls, internal factionalism and recurring border clashes with rival emirs in the south and east undermined civic defence against advancing Norman forces. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Siculo-Arabic, Byzantine Greek, Latin; Religion: Islam, Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1054; Disestablished: 1066; Preceded by: Emirate of Sicily

name: Emirate of Syracuse
label: sicilian taifas
description: The Emirate of Syracuse was an independent Muslim city-state established along south-eastern Sicily during the mid-eleventh-century dissolution of the Kalbid emirate. Governed from the island stronghold of Ortygia by the energetic commander Ibn al-Thumna, the emirate possessed formidable naval docks and commanded maritime transit through the Ionian Sea. Syracuse fought bitter internecine wars against Ibn al-Hawwas of Agrigento, prompting fateful military alliances with Norman mercenaries that inadvertently accelerated the Christian conquest of the entire island. \n\n Status: Sovereign taifa; Capital: Syracuse; Common languages: Siculo-Arabic, Byzantine Greek; Religion: Islam; Government: Military emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1054; Disestablished: 1063; Preceded by: Emirate of Sicily

name: County of Castell
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Castell was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire located in Lower Franconia to the east of Würzburg. Ruled by the comital House of Castell from their ancestral castle on the Steigerwald slopes, the territory governed dozens of agrarian villages and vineyards across the Main river watershed. The county successfully maintained its sovereign immediacy and membership in the Franconian College of Imperial Counts for over seven centuries until its mediatisation and incorporation into the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Castell; Common languages: German; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Lutheranism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Castell; Historical era: High Middle Ages to Early Modern era; Established: 1055; Disestablished: 1806; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Bavaria

name: Kingdom of Polonnaruwa
description: The Kingdom of Polonnaruwa was a medieval Sinhalese monarchy that re-established native rule across the island of Sri Lanka after King Vijayabahu I expelled the occupying Chola Empire. Governing from the inland capital of Polonnaruwa, the realm attained its cultural and geopolitical zenith under Parakramabahu I, who unified the island, constructed monumental hydraulic reservoirs and projected naval expeditions into southern India and Burma. Polonnaruwa flourished as a beacon of Theravada Buddhism until repeated foreign invasions triggered its decline in the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Polonnaruwa; Common languages: Sinhala, Pali; Religion: Theravada Buddhism; Government: Hereditary monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1055; Disestablished: 1232; Preceded by: Chola Empire, Principality of Ruhuna

name: Taifa of Segorbe
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Segorbe was an ephemeral Muslim principality established in the mountainous interior of eastern al-Andalus along the Palancia river valley. Emerging during the turbulent fragmentations that followed the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba, the small taifa guarded vital highland passes connecting the Valencian coast to the Aragonese frontier. Originating from the dynastic division of the ancient Purang-Guge realm by royal descendants of the Tibetan Empire, the kingdom commanded vital trans-Himalayan trade passes linking western Tibet with Nepal and northern India. name: Kingdom of Varendra

name: Kingdom of Bailleul

name: Marquisate of Provence
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Provence was a feudal frontier polity of the Holy Roman Empire established in the northern territories of the historic comital domain of Provence. Governed principally by the Counts of Toulouse following territorial partitions in the twelfth century, the realm maintained substantial autonomy along the Rhône valley. name: Naiman Confederation
description: The Naiman Confederation was a powerful nomadic tribal union that held sway over the steppes and mountain valleys of western Mongolia during the twelfth century. Following the expansion of the Western Liao, the confederacy acknowledged the suzerainty of the Qara Khitai Gurkhan while maintaining its seasonal encampments and ancestral military structure. name: Nilgiri State
description: Nilgiri State was an autonomous Hindu princely domain established in the coastal hinterland of modern Odisha. Founded by rulers of the Bhanj dynasty, the principality successfully maintained internal independence amidst fluctuating regional hegemonies across eastern India. Operating from its fortified seat at Raj Nilgiri, the state fostered local agricultural enterprise and regional religious traditions across several centuries of feudal self-rule. \n\n Status: Princely state; Capital: Nilagiri; Common languages: Odia and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhanj; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1126

name: Republic of Siena
label: holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Siena was an independent merchant commonwealth that exercised authority across southern Tuscany from the twelfth century onward. Governing through rotating councils of consuls and burghers from its urban core around the Piazza del Campo, the state emerged as a foremost banking and mercantile power in central Italy. Siena engaged in protracted economic and territorial rivalry with neighbouring Florence before submitting to foreign imperial forces in the mid-sixteenth century. \n\n Status: City-state republic; Capital: Siena; Common languages: Tuscan Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Merchant republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1126; Disestablished: 1559; Succeeded by: Duchy of Florence

name: Commune of Piacenza
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Piacenza was an autonomous northern Italian civic republic located near the strategic confluence of the Po and Trebbia rivers. Governed by elected consuls and trade guilds, the commune profited from its role as an essential crossing point along major transalpine and Emilian trade arteries. Piacenza vigorously defended its municipal privileges against imperial Hohenstaufen claims through active membership in the Lombard League. \n\n Status: Self-governing commune of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Piacenza; Common languages: Emilian Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1127; Succeeded by: Duchy of Milan

name: Great Chu
description: Great Chu was an ephemeral puppet kingdom created in northern China by the Jurchen Jin dynasty during the Jin–Song Wars. Following the capture of the Song capital of Kaifeng in 1127, Jin commanders placed former Song chancellor Zhang Bangchang on the imperial throne to administer unruly central territories without direct Jurchen occupation. The regime collapsed within a single month when Zhang yielded authority to Prince Zhao Gou, who re-established the Southern Song dynasty. \n\n Status: Puppet state of the Jin dynasty; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Autocratic monarchy; Head of state: Zhang Bangchang; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 5 October 1127; Disestablished: 1 November 1127; Succeeded by: Southern Song dynasty

name: County of Gorizia
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Gorizia was a feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire located across Friuli and the Isonzo valley. Ruled by the Meinhardiner dynasty from their ancestral stronghold at Gorizia, the comital house accumulated extensive lordships and advocate rights across the eastern Alps. The state developed as a vital crossroads connecting German, Friulian and Slavic populations before later passing to the Austrian House of Habsburg. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Gorizia; Common languages: German, Friulian, Slovene and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Meinhardiner; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1128

name: Lordship of Schelklingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Schelklingen was a compact noble domain of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Swabian Jura along the upper Danube valley. Held by local Swabian aristocrats from their castle near modern Ehingen, the territory exercised immediate imperial rights over nearby farming villages and forest tracts. The dynasty maintained autonomous judicial authority until comital debts and territorial consolidation led to its absorption by the House of Austria. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Schelklingen; Common languages: Swabian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1128; Disestablished: 1344; Succeeded by: Further Austria

name: Margraviate of Baden-Hachberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Baden-Hachberg was a German feudal principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Upper Rhine plain around Emmendingen. Formed as a partition of the wider Zähringer patrimony, the junior comital line ruled their lands from Hochburg castle while asserting immediate imperial sovereignty. The margraves successfully maintained autonomous administration and fortified footholds along the Black Forest foothills until the senior Baden line reacquired the territory in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Emmendingen; Common languages: Alemannic German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Zähringen; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1128; Disestablished: 1416; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Baden

name: Principality of Grodno
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Grodno was a western East Slavic appanage realm centred along the upper Neman river basin. Established by a branch of the Rurikid dynasty following the division of regional Kievan domains, the principality protected vital riverine trade corridors against Baltic Yotvingian and Lithuanian incursions. Its fortified citadel at Grodno served as an administrative and military strongpoint until gradual incorporation into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Rus appanage principality; Capital: Grodno; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1128; Disestablished: 1201; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Zengid Dynasty
description: The Zengid Dynasty governed a prominent Sunni Muslim atabegate founded across Upper Mesopotamia and northern Syria under nominal Great Seljuk suzerainty. Initiated by the military commander Imad al-Din Zengi from his seat at Mosul, the realm led energetic military campaigns against neighbouring Crusader settlements and rival regional emirs. The dynasty laid crucial administrative and ideological foundations for regional unification before Saladin established Ayyubid predominance across the Levant. \n\n Status: Atabegate under Great Seljuk suzerainty; Capital: Mosul; Common languages: Arabic, Persian and Oghuz Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military atabegate; Ruling dynasty: Zengid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1128; Succeeded by: Ayyubid Sultanate

name: County of Leiningen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Leiningen was an immediate feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire established in the Palatinate and northern Alsace. Ruled by the noble House of Leiningen from their fortress at Altleiningen, the county controlled important transport arteries and forested hill tracts across the Haardt mountains. Despite numerous partitions among family cadet branches across succeeding generations, the comital line retained its sovereign imperial immediacy until the French Revolutionary wars. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Altleiningen; Common languages: Rhine Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Leiningen; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1129

name: Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate
description: The Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate was a Karluk Turkic realm centred in the Tarim Basin and Semirechye, holding power from historic capitals including Kashgar and Balasagun. Subjugated as a tributary dependency following the westward migration and victory of the Qara Khitai in the early twelfth century, the khanate retained internal Islamic judicial structures under nomad oversight. Its dual administrative tradition preserved urban literary Turkic and Persian culture until final extinction by rival nomadic forces in 1212. \n\n Status: Vassal khanate of the Qara Khitai; Capital: Kashgar; Common languages: Karakhanid Turkic, Persian and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Semi-nomadic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kara-Khanid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1129; Disestablished: 1212; Succeeded by: Qara Khitai

name: Lordship of Steinfurt
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Steinfurt was a sovereign baronial estate of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Münsterland region of north-western Germany. Controlled by the noble House of Steinfurt from their water castle on the Aa river, the territory maintained judicial autonomy against the neighbouring Prince-Bishops of Münster. Through astute dynastic alliances and trade privileges, its rulers fostered urban development and defended their immediate imperial standing across the High Middle Ages. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Steinfurt; Common languages: Low German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1130; Succeeded by: County of Steinfurt

name: Great Qi
description: Great Qi was an administrative puppet kingdom established in northern China under the patronage of the Jurchen Jin empire. Governed by Liu Yu, a former Song official who ruled from the captured northern capital at Kaifeng, the state was designed as a buffer domain against Southern Song counter-offensives. Lacking popular domestic loyalty and suffering military reverses in the field, the regime was summarily abolished and annexed by Jin authorities in 1137. \n\n Status: Puppet state of the Jin dynasty; Capital: Kaifeng; Common languages: Middle Chinese; Religion: Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism; Government: Autocratic monarchy; Head of state: Liu Yu; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1 November 1130; Disestablished: 1 November 1137; Succeeded by: Jin dynasty

name: Kingdom of Sicily
label: norse/viking polities;norman polities in southern italy
description: The Kingdom of Sicily was a Mediterranean maritime monarchy created when the Norman count Roger II united the island of Sicily with his continental conquests across southern Italy. Governed from the cosmopolitan capital of Palermo, the kingdom melded Norman, Byzantine and Arab cultural and administrative institutions into one of the wealthiest realms in Christendom. Its royal navy secured dominant trade routes and extended offensive operations across North Africa and the central Mediterranean. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Palermo; Common languages: Sicilian, Latin, Arabic and Greek; Religion: Roman Catholicism, Greek Orthodoxy and Islam; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Hauteville; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 25 December 1130; Succeeded by: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

name: Commune of Jesi
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Jesi was an independent civic republic located in the Marche region along the lower valley of the Esino river. Governed by municipal magistrates and popular assemblies, the town flourished through robust market exchange between the Apennine interior and the nearby Adriatic coast. Renowned as the birthplace of Emperor Frederick II, Jesi preserved its civic liberties through changing alliances amidst regional Guelph and Ghibelline conflicts. \n\n Status: Self-governing commune of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Jesi; Common languages: Central Italian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Civic republic; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1131; Disestablished: 1434; Succeeded by: Papal States

name: Emirate of Ani
description: The Emirate of Ani was a Muslim principality established around the historic Bagratid capital of Ani in eastern Anatolia and the South Caucasus. Ruled by the Kurdish Shaddadid dynasty, the emirate contended with surrounding Georgian and Armenian Christian principalities as well as rival Turkic emirs. Despite intermittent capture by King David the Builder and his successors, the Shaddadids retained local control over the famed trading hub until Georgia permanently incorporated the city in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Ani; Common languages: Persian, Armenian, Arabic and Kurdish; Religion: Sunni Islam and Armenian Christianity; Government: Hereditary emirate; Ruling dynasty: Shaddadid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1131; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Georgia

name: Landgraviate of Lower Alsace
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Lower Alsace was an imperial jurisdiction and noble territory of the Holy Roman Empire centred along the northern Alsatian plain around Haguenau. Originally vested in the counts of Hüneburg before passing to the Prince-Bishops of Strasbourg, the territory oversaw regional courts and peacekeeping across the Rhine valley. The landgraviate gradually fragmented as Strasbourg secured free imperial city status and local baronial dynasties asserted autonomous feudal rights. \n\n Status: Landgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Haguenau; Common languages: Alemannic German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1131; Disestablished: 1275; Succeeded by: Landvogtei of Lower Alsace

name: Lordship of Schönburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Schönburg was an immediate noble estate of the Holy Roman Empire located along the Zwickauer Mulde river in Saxony. Governed by the noble House of Schönburg from their fortress at Glauchau, the dynasty held hereditary judicial rights over surrounding towns and rural settlements. Through skilful diplomacy during imperial conflicts, the family retained their sovereign privileges and distinctive feudal autonomy well into the early modern era. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Glauchau; Common languages: Upper Saxon German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Schönburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1131

name: Lordship of Arnstein
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Arnstein was a small imperial domain of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the eastern foothills of the Harz mountains. Ruled by the comital House of Arnstein from their fortress above the Wipper valley, the estate commanded strategic local roadways and agricultural villages. The family maintained sovereign baronial rights until dynastic extinction in the late fourteenth century resulted in its absorption by neighbouring regional principalities. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Arnstein; Common languages: Middle Low German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1132; Disestablished: 1388; Succeeded by: County of Mansfeld

name: Lordship of Büdingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Büdingen was an autonomous noble territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Wetterau region of modern Hesse. Established by local counts who fortified the settlement of Büdingen with stone ramparts and a moated castle, the domain prospered through controlled river crossings and regional forest rights. Following the extinction of the male line at the start of the fourteenth century, the lordship was partitioned among the House of Isenburg and allied lineages. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Buedingen; Common languages: Central German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1132; Disestablished: 1305; Succeeded by: County of Isenburg-Büdingen

name: County of Wertheim
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Wertheim was a sovereign territorial state of the Holy Roman Empire located at the confluence of the Main and Tauber rivers in Franconia. Ruled by the comital House of Wertheim from their imposing hilltop fortress, the state commanded lucrative riverine customs and market rights. The counts played a prominent role in imperial politics and regional governance until the senior dynasty died out in the sixteenth century, after which the lands passed to collaterals before modern mediatisation. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Wertheim; Common languages: East Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Wertheim; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1807; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Baden

name: Kingdom of Qocho
description: The Kingdom of Qocho was a Buddhist and Manichaean Uyghur realm established across the Turpan Depression and eastern slopes of the Tian Shan. While maintaining summer and winter residences at Beshbalik and Qocho, the royal court accepted vassal status under the non-Muslim Qara Khitai Khaganate during the twelfth century. Its cosmopolitan oasis cities fostered flourishing Silk Road commerce, translation centres and architectural achievements before voluntarily submitting to Genghis Khan in 1209. \n\n Status: Vassal kingdom of the Qara Khitai; Capital: Qocho; Common languages: Old Uyghur, Middle Chinese, Tocharian and Sogdian; Religion: Buddhism, Manichaeism and Church of the East; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruler title: Idiqut; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1210; Succeeded by: Mongol Empire

name: Lord Novgorod the Great
label: russian principalities
description: Lord Novgorod the Great was an expansive merchant republic in north-western Russia that broke away from Kievan authority following the expulsion of its prince in 1136. Governed through a general assembly known as the veche, alongside an elected mayor and archbishop, the state controlled vast subarctic territories stretching eastward to the Ural Mountains. Its commercial prosperity was anchored in the Baltic fur and timber trade through extensive connections with the Hanseatic League. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Veliky Novgorod; Common languages: Old East Slavic and Old Novgorod dialect; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Merchant republic; Legislature: Veche; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1243; Succeeded by: Novgorod Republic (Mongol vassal)

name: Principality of Chernigov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Chernigov was one of the largest and most influential East Slavic realms to emerge from the fragmentation of Kievan Rus'. Ruled by the Olgovichi branch of the Rurikid dynasty, the state commanded a vast territory across northern Ukraine, western Russia and eastern Belarus. Its princes frequently contested supreme authority over Kiev while enriching their riverine capitals with monumental brick cathedrals until devastating Mongol invasions shattered the realm in 1240. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Chernihiv; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Olgovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1240; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Principality of Halych
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Halych was a southwestern Rus principality situated in the northern foothills of the Carpathian Mountains along the Dniester river basin. Ruled by the descendants of Rostislav of Tmutarakan, the realm developed a distinctive political system characterised by a powerful boyar council that often placed sharp limits on the prince's authority. Its strategic borderland position facilitated active commerce and diplomacy with Poland and Hungary before its union with Volhynia around 1200. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Halych; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rostislavichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1200; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia

name: Principality of Kiev
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kiev was an East Slavic realm that encompassed the historic heartland of Kievan Rus' around the middle Dnieper valley. As outer provinces asserted sovereign independence following the death of Mstislav the Great, the reduced princely domain became the focal point of bitter dynastic conflicts among rival Rurikid branches for the prestige of the Grand Princely title. Despite diminished territorial size, the city remained the spiritual capital of Rus' until sacked by the Mongols in 1240. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Kyiv; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1241; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Principality of Kursk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kursk was a Rus appanage principality situated along the Seym river on the forest-steppe frontier of the Severian lands. Governed by a cadet line of the Olgovichi house of Chernigov, the realm served as an essential military shield against recurrent nomad incursions from the southern steppes. Its fortified capital at Kursk supported agricultural settlements and iron extraction until successive Polovtsian clashes and the thirteenth-century Mongol invasion crippled the local dynastic seat. \n\n Status: Rus appanage principality; Capital: Kursk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Olgovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1276; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Principality of Novgorod-Seversk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Novgorod-Seversk was a Severian realm situated along the Desna river that detached from Chernigov under the rule of Prince Sviatoslav Olgovich. The principality played a central role in guarding the eastern flanks of the Rus' against nomadic Polovtsian raiders, an arduous campaign celebrated in the epic Tale of Igor's Campaign. Its princes maintained autonomous military retinues and distinct mints before Mongol conquest relegated the principality to appanage status under Briansk and Lithuania. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Novhorod-Siverskyi; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Olgovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1363; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Peremyshl
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Peremyshl was a western Rus principality centred on the San river in the historic region of Red Ruthenia. Established as an appanage for the elder sons of the Rostislavichi dynasty, the realm controlled vital trans-Carpathian transit corridors linking Rus' with the Kingdom of Poland and the Kingdom of Hungary. In the mid-twelfth century, Prince Volodymyrko Volodarovych unified Peremyshl with neighbouring petty principalities to forge the consolidated Principality of Halych. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Przemyśl; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rostislavichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1142; Succeeded by: Principality of Halych

name: Principality of Pereyaslavl
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Pereyaslavl was an East Slavic frontier realm located east of the middle Dnieper along the Trubizh river. Positioned directly on the nomadic steppe frontier, the principality bore the initial brunt of Pecheneg and Cuman incursions while shielding the core territories of Kiev. Its rulers, drawn from the Monomakhovichi dynasty, maintained strong military fortresses and ecclesiastical centres until the catastrophic Mongol campaign destroyed the capital in 1239. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Pereiaslav; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Monomakhovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1 April 1238; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Principality of Pronsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Pronsk was an appanage territory located in the forest-steppe basin of the Pronya river, functioning as a constituent realm of the wider Principality of Ryazan. Established by a branch of the local Rurikid dynasty, the principality defended the southern borders of north-eastern Rus' against steppe raiders while frequently contesting dynastic primacy with Ryazan. Pronsk maintained its fortified citadel and local assemblies until final absorption by the Grand Principality of Moscow. \n\n Status: Rus appanage principality; Capital: Pronsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1484; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Moscow

name: Principality of Rostov-Suzdal
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Rostov-Suzdal was a northern East Slavic state in the fertile agricultural region between the Oka and Volga rivers. Under Prince Yuri Dolgorukiy, who transferred his court from Rostov to Suzdal, the realm expanded rapidly through the settlement of new fortified towns and the establishment of independent administrative networks. This period laid the territorial and political foundations for the Grand Principality of Vladimir when Andrei Bogolyubsky shifted the capital southward in 1157. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Suzdal; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Monomakhovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1158; Succeeded by: Grand Principality of Vladimir

name: Principality of Ryazan
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Ryazan was an independent East Slavic realm situated in the upper Oka basin that separated from the Murom-Chernigov lands in the early twelfth century. Administered from its fortified citadel at Old Ryazan, the state oversaw vital riverine trade while developing strong local defensive forces to resist steppe nomad raids. Its strategic position placed it directly in the path of the Mongol invasion, which decimated the old capital in 1237 and forced submission to the Golden Horde. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Staraya Ryazan; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1238; Succeeded by: Golden Horde

name: Principality of Smolensk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Smolensk was a sovereign East Slavic state controlling the strategic portages between the upper Dnieper, Western Dvina and Volga river basins. Under the leadership of Prince Rostislav Mstislavich and his successors, the principality grew into a wealthy commercial and ecclesiastical powerhouse linked to Baltic and Black Sea trade. The realm maintained autonomous diplomatic ties across eastern Europe until internal divisions and western expansion led to its incorporation into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Smolensk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Russian Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rostislavichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1243; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Terebovlia
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Terebovlia was an early southwestern Rus appanage situated along the Hnizna and Seret rivers in eastern Galicia. Held by Prince Vasylko Rostyslavych and his descendants, the territory was heavily fortified to counter nomadic Cuman incursions and resist Hungarian expansion across the Carpathians. In the 1140s, the principality was unified with the neighbouring lands of Peremyshl and Zvenyhorod to create the formidable consolidated Principality of Halych. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Terebovlia; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rostislavichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1142; Succeeded by: Principality of Halych

name: Principality of Tmutarakan
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Tmutarakan was an isolated East Slavic enclave centred on the Taman Peninsula commanding the Cimmerian Bosporus between the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Controlling ancient maritime routes that connected the Rus' lands with the Byzantine Empire and the Caucasus, the port hosted a diverse population of Slavs, Greeks, Khazars and Alans. As nomadic Kipchak tribes cut overland contact with the northern principalities, local Rus' administration faded under Byzantine and nomadic influence. \n\n Status: Sovereign Rus principality; Capital: Taman; Common languages: Old East Slavic, Medieval Greek and Khazar; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1133; Disestablished: 1170; Succeeded by: Cuman-Kipchak Confederation

name: Principality of Turov
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Turov was an East Slavic realm established across the extensive Pripyat Marshes of modern southern Belarus and northern Ukraine. Originally governed as an appanage closely linked to the Grand Princes of Kiev, the territory gained substantial autonomy under local Rurikid princes who developed important riverine trading settlements. description: The Marquisate of Clavesana was a sovereign feudal principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Ligurian Alps and southern Piedmont. Formed from the partition of the vast Aleramici patrimony of Bonifacio del Vasto, the realm was governed by Marquis Ugo and his successors from their cliffside stronghold overlooking the Tanaro river. The marquisate exploited natural rocky gorges to build an impregnable mountain bastion, controlling transalpine trade between the Po Valley and the Ligurian coast until absorbed by neighbouring communes and Montferrat. \n\n Status: Margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Clavesana; Common languages: Piedmontese, Ligurian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: Aleramici; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1143; Disestablished: 1398; Succeeded by: Marquisate of Montferrat

label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Saluzzo was an autonomous feudal state of the Holy Roman Empire located in south-western Piedmont and adjacent valleys of the French Alps. Established by the Aleramici dynasty under Manfred I, the marquisate commanded vital transalpine passes connecting the Po plain with the Kingdom of France and Dauphiné. name: Atabegate of Azerbaijan
