Initially rising as governors and guardians for junior Seljuk princes, the Eldiguzid dynasty established de facto independence from seats at Nakhchivan, Tabriz and Hamadan, controlling trade across Arran and Iranian Azerbaijan. The atabegs patronised Persian court poetry and defended their northern borders against Georgia until the western incursions of the Khwarazmians and Mongols brought down the dynasty. \n\n Status: Sovereign atabegate; Capital: Nakhchivan; Common languages: Persian, Oghuz Turkic and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Military atabegate; Ruling dynasty: Eldiguzid; Ruler title: Atabeg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1144; Disestablished: 1225; Succeeded by: Khwarazmian Empire

name: County of Hanau
label: holy roman empire;confederation of the rhine
description: The County of Hanau was an immediate feudal territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the fertile Main-Kinzig basin east of Frankfurt. Evolving from a medieval baronial lordship into an imperial county, the House of Hanau governed extensive agricultural estates, market towns and riverine trade routes from their city residence. Despite subsequent partitions into the distinct branches of Hanau-Münzenberg and Hanau-Lichtenberg, the comital domains retained imperial immediacy until the extinction of the male lines in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Hanau; Common languages: Rhine Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hanau; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1144; Disestablished: 1737; Succeeded by: Landgraviate of Hesse-Kassel

name: County of Jülich
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Jülich was an autonomous territorial principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Rur river between the Meuse and the Rhine. Centred on the historic Roman settlement of Jülich, the comital dynasty expanded their authority over neighbouring lowlands through energetic military alliances and lucrative agricultural tolls. The counts vigorously defended their immediate imperial standing against the rival archbishops of Cologne, progressively elevating the territory into a margraviate and duchy before uniting with the County of Berg. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Jülich; Common languages: Ripuarian Low Franconian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Jülich; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1144; Disestablished: 1337; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Jülich

name: Taifa of Constantina and Hornachuelos
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Constantina and Hornachuelos was an ephemeral Muslim emirate established in the Sierra Morena uplands of western al-Andalus during the collapse of Almoravid rule. Operating from fortified hill towns north of Seville, local Andalusi leaders asserted autonomous authority over surrounding olive orchards, grazing hills and regional mining operations. The taifa maintained precarious independence against Christian incursions and rival Muslim factions before being subjugated and annexed by the newly arrived Almohad Caliphate around 1151. \n\n Status: Independent taifa emirate; Capital: Constantina; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1144; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Lordship of Dornberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Dornberg was an immediate noble territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Starkenburg region around modern Darmstadt in southern Hesse. Ruled by the noble House of Dornberg from their moated ancestral castle, the domain exercised territorial jurisdiction over adjacent agricultural manors and extensive woodlands along the Rhine plain. The lordship preserved its sovereign status and judicial rights until the extinction of the male line in 1257 led to its transmission to the Counts of Katzenelnbogen. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Darmstadt; Common languages: Rhine Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Dornberg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 18 October 1144; Disestablished: 1332; Succeeded by: County of Katzenelnbogen

name: Angevin Empire
description: The Angevin Empire was a composite dynastic monarchy assembled by King Henry II of England, encompassing the Kingdom of England, the Duchy of Normandy, Anjou, Maine and Touraine. Following Henry's marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine, the Plantagenet crown exercised authority over roughly half of France alongside Ireland and Wales, holding court primarily on the continent at Angers and Chinon. While owing nominal feudal homage to the French Capetian monarchy for their continental fiefs, the Plantagenet rulers operated as an autonomous European super-power. \n\n Status: Composite feudal monarchy; Administrative seat: Angers; Common languages: Anglo-Norman, Old French and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal composite monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Plantagenet; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1 December 1154; Succeeded by: Angevin Empire (consolidated)

name: Burgraviate of Dohna
label: holy roman empire
description: The Burgraviate of Dohna was an imperial frontier principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Müglitz valley south of Dresden in the Saxon borderlands. Entrusted to the noble Donin family by the Emperor to secure Bohemian-Saxon border passes, the burgraves exercised immediate territorial sovereignty, judicial rights and mineral privileges over the Eastern Ore Mountains. The dynasty stoutly preserved its autonomous authority against the expansionist Margraves of Meissen until defeated in the protracted Dohna Feud in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Burgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Dohna; Common languages: Upper Saxon German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal burgraviate; Ruling dynasty: House of Dohna; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1403; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Meissen

name: County of Hohenberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Hohenberg was an influential Swabian noble state of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the upper Neckar valley around Rottenburg. Emerging as a cadet branch of the House of Hohenzollern, the counts established an independent territorial principality characterised by the founding of several collegiate churches and monasteries. In the thirteenth century, the family achieved high imperial prominence when Gertrude of Hohenberg married King Rudolf of Habsburg, though financial insolvency eventually compelled the sale of their comital core to Austria in 1381. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Rottenburg am Neckar; Common languages: Swabian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Hohenberg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1382; Succeeded by: Further Austria

name: Lordship of Homburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Homburg was an immediate noble domain of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Weser Uplands near Stadtoldendorf in modern Lower Saxony. Governed from the fortified hilltop castle of Hohenbüchen and later the Homburg fortress, the noble Lords of Homburg exercised judicial authority over surrounding timberlands, pastures and farming villages. The family maintained imperial immediacy and baronial privileges across several centuries until the male lineage died out in 1409, after which the lands were acquired by the House of Welf. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Stadtoldendorf; Common languages: Middle Low German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Homburg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1410; Succeeded by: Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel

name: Prince-Bishopric of Havelberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Havelberg was an ecclesiastical state of the Holy Roman Empire located at the confluence of the Havel and Elbe rivers. Following the Wendish Crusade in the mid-twelfth century, the bishops established effective temporal sovereignty over the surrounding Slavic frontier territories, ruling from their fortified cathedral precinct at Havelberg. The prince-bishops oversaw Christianisation, dike construction and agrarian settlement until the spread of the Protestant Reformation led to the secularisation and eventual annexation of the bishopric by the Margraves of Brandenburg. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Havelberg; Common languages: Middle Low German, Polabian and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Prince-bishopric; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1572; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Brandenburg

name: Taifa of Beja and Évora
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Beja and Évora was an autonomous Muslim principality that arose in the Alentejo plains of south-western Iberia following the retreat of Almoravid imperial power. Centred on the fortified Roman citadel of Beja and the ancient walled city of Évora, the taifa controlled extensive wheat fields, olive groves and livestock pastures. Local Andalusi rulers struggled to secure defensive alliances against predatory Christian raids from Portugal and rival Moorish factions before being conquered and incorporated by the Almohad Caliphate around 1151. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Beja; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Taifa of Jerez
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Jerez was a short-lived Andalusi city-state established around the fortified town of Jerez de la Frontera in south-western Spain during the second taifa era. Led by local military chieftains of the Banu Khazraj tribe, the emirate oversaw rich vineyards, olive estates and salt marshes near the mouth of the Guadalete river. The regime maintained a tenuous regional sovereignty amidst regional civil warfare before capitulating to the rapid military expansion of the Almohad Caliphate. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Jerez de la Frontera; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Khazraj; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1146; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Taifa of Santarém
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Santarém was an ephemeral Muslim city-state established in the fertile lower Tagus valley of central Portugal during the fragmentation of the Almoravid Empire. Governed by Arab elites from the Banu Khazraj clan from their imposing citadel on the bluffs of Santarém, the taifa held jurisdiction over riverside agricultural orchards and river traffic. Confronted by mounting pressure from the nascent Kingdom of Portugal under Afonso Henriques, the town was annexed by the neighbouring Taifa of Badajoz before falling to Christian conquest. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Santarém; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Khazraj; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1145; Disestablished: 1146; Succeeded by: Taifa of Badajoz

name: Taifa of Guadix and Baza
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Guadix and Baza was an autonomous Andalusi emirate established in the rugged plateau country of eastern Granada between the Sierra Nevada and the Sierra de Baza. Exploiting the administrative collapse of Almoravid rule, local Muslim notables governed the twin mountain basins and organised the defence of traditional troglodyte settlements and terraced irrigation networks. The small state enjoyed only a brief span of independence before falling under the dominion of the expanding Taifa of Murcia under Muhammad ibn Mardanish. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Guadix; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1146; Disestablished: 1152; Succeeded by: Taifa of Murcia

name: Taifa of Purchena
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Purchena was a small Moorish principality centred on the fortified valley of the Almanzora river in modern Almería in south-eastern Spain. Administered by local leaders of the Banu Khazraj lineage from the hill castle of Purchena, the taifa oversaw regional marble quarries, olive terraces and defensive watchtowers. Surrounded by competing warlords and threatened by Christian frontier incursions, the enclave was swiftly subjugated and absorbed into the growing regional realm of the Taifa of Murcia. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Purchena; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Khazraj; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1146; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Taifa of Murcia

name: County Palatine of Tübingen
label: holy roman empire
description: The County Palatine of Tübingen was a prominent territorial principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in the central Neckar valley of Swabia. Rising to prominence from their ancestral castle of Hohentübingen, the counts palatine exercised hereditary imperial prerogatives, founded renowned monastic houses like Bebenhausen Abbey and governed extensive Swabian lands. However, lavish court expenditures and recurrent territorial partitions among cadet lines precipitated economic decline, compelling the sale of their capital to the Counts of Württemberg in the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: County palatine of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Tübingen; Common languages: Swabian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Tübingen; Ruler title: Count Palatine; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1147; Disestablished: 1347; Succeeded by: County of Württemberg

name: Lordship of Signau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Signau was an immediate baronial territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the upper Emmental valley in modern Switzerland. Ruled by the noble Barons of Signau from their fortified castle, the estate controlled agricultural pasture lands, timber reserves and trade routes connecting the Swiss plateau with the Bernese Oberland. The dynasty preserved its baronial independence and judicial rights across the High Middle Ages until financial difficulties led to its sale to the expanding city-state of Bern in 1530. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Signau; Common languages: Alemannic German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1147; Disestablished: 1530; Succeeded by: Canton of Bern

name: Principality of Putivl
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Putivl was an East Slavic appanage realm located along the Seym river in the Severian borderland between Rus' and the wild steppe. Formed as a subdivision of the Principality of Novgorod-Seversk, Putivl guarded critical eastern river crossings and supplied vital warrior detachments for campaigns against the nomadic Polovtsians. Its fortified citadel held high symbolic importance in early East Slavic literature, maintaining local dynastic governance until absorption into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later Muscovy. \n\n Status: Rus appanage principality; Capital: Putyvl; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Olgovichi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1147; Disestablished: 1501; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Taifa of Tavira
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Tavira was a short-lived maritime emirate established in the eastern Algarve along the mouth of the Gilão river in southern Portugal. Founded during the general revolt against Almoravid rule, local Muslim commanders utilised the sheltered lagoon harbour of Tavira to oversee coastal fishing, salt panning and regional coastal trade. The tiny taifa lacked the defensive manpower to maintain lasting autonomy and was absorbed by the advancing armies of the Almohad Caliphate around 1151. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Tavira; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1147; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Taifa of Tejada
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Tejada was an autonomous Andalusi principality centred on the fortified ancient town of Tejada in the modern province of Huelva in south-western Spain. Governed by Emir Yusuf al-Bitruyi, who also held authority in neighbouring Niebla, the realm controlled fertile cereal lands and trade approaches toward the lower Guadalquivir basin. The emirate retained fragile independence amidst the political vacuum following Almoravid decline before being overrun and incorporated into the Almohad Empire around 1151. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Tejada; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Ruling dynasty: Banu Bitruy; Ruler title: Emir; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1147; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Almohad Caliphate

name: Burgraviate of Altenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Burgraviate of Altenburg was an imperial office and sovereign territory of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Pleissnerland south of Leipzig. Entrusted by the Hohenstaufen emperors to imperial burgraves who governed from the fortified imperial castle at Altenburg, the domain secured trade roads and colonised Slavic lands east of the Saale. The burgraves maintained immediate imperial jurisdiction and defensive leadership across the region until political rivalries and financial decline led to the annexation of the territory by the House of Wettin. \n\n Status: Burgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Altenburg; Common languages: Upper Saxon German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal burgraviate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 1330; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Meissen

name: Couto Misto
description: Couto Misto was an autonomous border microstate situated in the rugged Salas Valley along the frontier between the Kingdom of Portugal and the Kingdom of Galicia. Comprising the three historic villages of Santiago de Rubiás, Rubiás and Meaus, the community developed out of complex medieval feudal immunities that placed it outside the direct jurisdiction of both neighbouring crowns. Its inhabitants enjoyed unique sovereignty, electing their own judge, exercising complete tax exemption and maintaining asylum rights until partitioned by the 1864 Treaty of Lisbon. \n\n Status: Independent microstate; Capital: Santiago de Rubiás; Common languages: Galician and Portuguese; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Direct democracy and popular assembly; Ruler title: Judge; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 29 September 1864; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Spain and Kingdom of Portugal

name: Cutch State
description: Cutch State was an independent maritime kingdom situated along the Gulf of Kutch and the Rann of Kutch salt flats in western India. Founded by the Jadeja Rajput dynasty, who migrated from Sindh and established their seat at Lakhiarviro and later Bhuj, the realm prospered through extensive sea trade with Arabia, the Persian Gulf and East Africa. The rulers commanded strong naval flotillas and desert cavalry forces, fiercely guarding their political sovereignty against surrounding sultanates until entering subsidiary alliance with the British in 1819. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Bhuj; Common languages: Kutchi, Gujarati and Sindhi; Religion: Hinduism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Jadeja; Ruler title: Maharao; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 1820; Succeeded by: Cutch (British protectorate)

name: Free Imperial City of Giengen
label: holy roman empire
description: The Free Imperial City of Giengen was a self-governing civic republic of the Holy Roman Empire situated along the Brenz river on the eastern edge of the Swabian Alb. Granted imperial immediacy by the Hohenstaufen emperors, the town governed its domestic affairs through an elected municipal council and guild magistrates without submitting to local noble overlords. Giengen flourished as a manufacturing centre for linens and metalwork along the trade route to Nuremberg, maintaining its republican independence until mediatised to the Kingdom of Württemberg in 1803. \n\n Status: Free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Giengen an der Brenz; Common languages: Swabian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Imperial city republic; Legislature: City Council; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 25 February 1803; Succeeded by: Kingdom of Württemberg

name: Margraviate of Burgau
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Burgau was an autonomous territorial principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in Swabian Bavaria along the Mindel and Danube rivers. Governed by the comital House of Berg-Schelklingen, the rulers adopted the title of margrave and held immediate imperial jurisdiction over fertile agricultural manors, woodlands and fortified market towns. The margraviate maintained substantial political standing in south-western Germany until mounting debts prompted the sale of the entire estate to the House of Habsburg in the late fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Burgau; Common languages: Swabian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Berg-Schelklingen; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 1379; Succeeded by: Further Austria

name: Principality of Kletsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Kletsk was a western East Slavic appanage realm located around the upper Lan river basin in modern south-western Belarus. Partitioned from the wider Principality of Turov and Pinsk, the territory was ruled by local Rurikid princes who defended the frontier between Polotsk, Volhynia and the pagan Baltic tribes. Its fortified wooden kremlin at Kletsk served as an administrative and trade centre until the gradual incorporation of the appanage into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania during the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Rus appanage principality; Capital: Kletsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurikid; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 1401; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Taifa of Segura
label: spanish taifas
description: The Taifa of Segura was an independent Moorish principality established around the hill fortress of Segura de la Sierra in the rugged mountain ranges of eastern Andalusia. Formed during the widespread anti-Almoravid uprisings, the taifa held command over heavily wooded valleys, olive groves and strategic mountain passages connecting Andalusia with the Levantine coast. The emirate retained sovereign authority for only a brief period before being subdued and integrated into the emerging realm of the Taifa of Murcia around 1151. \n\n Status: Independent taifa kingdom; Capital: Segura; Common languages: Andalusi Arabic and Mozarabic; Religion: Islam; Government: Petty emirate; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Disestablished: 1151; Succeeded by: Taifa of Murcia

name: County of Ziegenhain
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Ziegenhain was an immediate comital principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Schwalm river basin of northern Hesse. Ruled by the comital House of Ziegenhain from their water fortress at modern Schwalmstadt, the state held vital territorial choke points and advocate rights connecting lower Hesse with the Rhine-Main region. The counts successfully asserted their sovereignty against the Landgraves of Hesse through protracted military feuds until the comital lineage died out in 1450, leading to its annexation by Hesse. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Schwalmstadt; Common languages: Hessian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ziegenhain; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1149; Disestablished: 1451; Succeeded by: Landgraviate of Hesse

name: Lordship of Erbach
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Erbach was an immediate noble estate of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Odenwald hills of southern Hesse. Held by the ancient House of Erbach from their castle on the Mümling river, the lords exercised sovereign territorial and judicial authority over densely forested uplands and farming settlements. The dynasty maintained baronial autonomy against surrounding regional powers through loyal service to the Holy Roman Emperors, eventually expanding their holdings until elevated to imperial comital status in 1532. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Erbach; Common languages: Rhine Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Erbach; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1149; Disestablished: 1533; Succeeded by: County of Erbach

name: Raugraviate
label: holy roman empire
description: The Raugraviate comprised the immediate feudal lands of the Holy Roman Empire held by the Raugraves along the Nahe and Alsenz river valleys in the Rhenish Palatinate. Descended from the ancient comital house of the Emichones, the Raugraves derived their distinctive title from the wild, uncultivated nature of their mountainous domain and governed from their ancestral stronghold at Altenbaumburg. The dynasty exercised sovereign territorial jurisdiction and imperial advocacy until lineage partitions and fiscal strain led to the absorption of their castles by neighbouring principalities. \n\n Status: Comital domain of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Altenbaumburg; Common languages: Rhine Franconian German and Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Raugraves; Ruler title: Raugrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1149; Disestablished: 1458; Succeeded by: Electoral Palatinate

name: Kingdom of Rapa Nui
description: The Kingdom of Rapa Nui was an isolated Polynesian island monarchy established on Easter Island in the south-eastern Pacific Ocean. Governed by a sacred hereditary monarch styled the Ariki Mau, who traced his lineage from the founding ancestor Hotu Matu'a, the society was organised into distinct clan territories centred around religious ceremonial platforms. Across the twelfth to sixteenth centuries, the kingdom mobilised sophisticated quarrying and stone transport methods to erect monumental stone moai along the coast before environmental pressures altered traditional governance. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Hanga Roa; Common languages: Rapa Nui; Religion: Polynesian religion and ancestor veneration; Government: Divine monarchy; Ruler title: Ariki Mau; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1150; Disestablished: 1501; Succeeded by: Rapa Nui tribal chiefdoms

name: Akure
label: yoruba kingdoms
description: Akure was an independent Yoruba kingdom established in the forested heartland of south-western Nigeria. Governed by a divine monarch bearing the royal title of Deji from his palace complex at Akure, the state exercised authority through traditional town councils and hereditary chieftaincies. The kingdom fostered agricultural trade in yams and palm products, maintaining its political sovereignty and distinctive cultural traditions through shifting regional alliances with the neighbouring kingdoms of Benin and Oyo until the late nineteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Akure (State); Common languages: Yoruba; Religion: Yoruba traditional religion; Government: Traditional absolute monarchy; Ruler title: Deji; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1151; Disestablished: 1891; Succeeded by: British Protectorate of Southern Nigeria

name: Bonai State
description: Bonai State was an autonomous Hindu princely domain located along the Brahmani river in the rugged, forested uplands of modern northern Odisha. Governed by the Kadamba Rajput dynasty from their fortified capital at Bonaigarh, the state held sway over extensive tribal populations, timber reserves and iron-bearing hills. The rulers preserved internal independence from neighbouring regional empires through difficult jungle topography and martial alliances, governing as a sovereign feudal monarchy until entering treaty relations with the British East India Company. \n\n Status: Sovereign princely state; Capital: Bonaigarh; Common languages: Odia, Ho and Mundari; Religion: Hinduism and tribal animism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Kadamba; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1151; Disestablished: 1802; Succeeded by: Bonai (British protectorate)

name: Cempoala
label: mesoamerican polities
description: Cempoala was a flourishing Mesoamerican city-state established by the Totonac people along the flat coastal plain of modern Veracruz near the Gulf of Mexico. Supported by sophisticated irrigation canals fed by the Actopan river, the metropolis developed into the political capital of Totonacapan, accommodating thousands of inhabitants within walled precincts of plastered temples and palaces. The city maintained sovereign independence and robust agricultural commerce until the fifteenth century, when the Aztec Triple Alliance conquered the region and imposed heavy tribute obligations. \n\n Status: Sovereign city-state; Capital: Cempoala; Common languages: Totonac and Nahuatl; Religion: Mesoamerican polytheism; Government: Theocratic city-state monarchy; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1151; Disestablished: 1470; Succeeded by: Aztec Empire

name: Chero Dynasty
description: The Chero Dynasty was an indigenous tribal realm that governed extensive territories across the Chota Nagpur plateau and the Son river valley in present-day Bihar and Jharkhand. Rising to regional prominence following the disintegration of the Pala Empire, the Chero chieftains ruled from fortified stone strongholds at Palamu Forts, controlling vital transit routes through the forested hills. name: Keonjhar State

name: Kingdom of Mewar

name: Sena Dynasty

name: Commune of Castellaro

name: Prince-Bishopric of Geneva

label: holy roman empire

name: Commune of Faenza
label: holy roman empire

name: Duchy of Limburg

Evolving from a strategic eleventh-century county of Lower Lotharingia, the realm was elevated to ducal status as its rulers contested regional supremacy against neighbouring Brabant and the archbishops of Cologne. name: Kingdom of Sweden
description: The Kingdom of Sweden was an expanding medieval Scandinavian realm encompassing Svealand and Götaland around Lakes Mälaren and Vättern. Solidified through the consolidation of provincial law-codes and royal authority during the alternating reigns of the Sverker and Eric dynasties, the kingdom expanded eastward across the Baltic into Finland through royal crusades. name: Prince-Bishopric of Constance

Holding imperial immediacy alongside a vast spiritual diocese that stretched across Swabia and northern Switzerland, the prince-bishops exercised temporal rule over several non-contiguous districts and market towns. The episcopal administration weathered the Reformation, during which the court relocated its residency across the lake to Meersburg, preserving its imperial estate status until secularisation in 1803. \n\n Status: Prince-Bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Konstanz; Common languages: Alemannic German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1803; Succeeded by: Electorate of Baden

The Babenberg dukes expanded their influence into neighbouring Styria before the extinction of their male line in 1246 initiated decades of regional succession warfare. \n\n Status: Duchy of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Vienna; Common languages: Austro-Bavarian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal duchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Babenberg; Ruler title: Duke of Austria; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 17 September 1156; Preceded by: Margraviate of Austria

name: Imperial Abbey of Fulda
label: holy roman empire
description: The Imperial Abbey of Fulda was an ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire located in eastern Hesse along the Fulda river. Originating as a celebrated eighth-century Benedictine monastery containing the shrine of Saint Boniface, the abbey secured imperial immediacy and developed substantial temporal lordships across central Germany. Its abbots were recognised as princes of the empire in 1221 and later invested with the ceremonial dignity of archchancellors to the empress, maintaining territorial sovereignty until elevated to a prince-bishopric in the eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Princely Abbey of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Fulda; Common languages: Hessian and German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Abbot; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Rhenish Franconia; Disestablished: 1752

name: Jaisalmer State
description: Jaisalmer State was a Bhati Rajput kingdom established in 1156 in the arid heart of the Thar Desert in western Rajasthan. Founded by Maharawal Jaisal after shifting his ancestral capital from Lodhruva to a fortified yellow sandstone ridge, the kingdom commanded vital overland caravan routes connecting northern India with Sindh and Central Asia. The desert monarchy endured centuries of siege warfare and frontier raids from neighbouring sultanates while maintaining unbroken dynastic autonomy until signing a subsidiary alliance with the British in 1818. \n\n Status: Sovereign kingdom; Capital: Jaisalmer; Common languages: Marwari, Rajasthani and Sanskrit; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Bhati Rajput; Ruler title: Maharawal; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1156

name: Principality of Vshchizh
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Vshchizh was a medieval East Slavic appanage state centred on the fortified town of Vshchizh along the Desna river in the Chernigov lands. Created during dynastic divisions among the Olgovichi princes of Chernigov in 1157, the principality briefly functioned as an active regional centre of craft production and military organisation. Its autonomy came to an abrupt end during the Mongol invasion of Rus in 1239, when the fortress was completely razed and its territory reabsorbed into neighbouring appanages. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Vshchizh; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1157; Disestablished: 1240

name: Artuqids
description: The Artuqids were an Oghuz Turkoman dynasty that governed Upper Mesopotamia and portions of northern Syria following the decentralisation of the Seljuk Empire. Divided into prominent branches centred at Mardin and Hasankeyf, the rulers created an enduring regional hegemony celebrated for monumental stone architecture, innovative copper coinage and intellectual patronage. They skilfully preserved their territorial autonomy amidst fierce rivalries involving Crusader states, the Zengids and the Ayyubids until falling to rival Turkoman confederacies in the early fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Mardin; Common languages: Oghuz Turkic, Arabic and Syriac; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1102; Succeeded by: Qara Qoyunlu

name: Beylik of Dilmaç
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Beylik of Dilmaç was an early Anatolian Turkic principality centred on the rugged mountain redoubt of Bitlis and the adjacent town of Erzen in eastern Anatolia. Established following the Battle of Manzikert, the dynasty achieved complete autonomy after the fragmentation of the Great Seljuk Empire under rulers such as Togan Arslan. The beylik maintained a formidable martial reputation, participating in regional campaigns against Crusader armies and neighbouring lords until succumbing to larger regional powers during the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign beylik; Capital: Bitlis; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Anatolia

name: Commune of Orvieto
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Orvieto was a fortified city-state in southwestern Umbria, dramatically perched atop a massive volcanic tuff plateau rising above the Paglia valley. Establishing communal self-government during the twelfth century, the republic expanded its territorial control across southern Tuscany and the Chiana valley while forging a staunch alliance with the Papacy. The city prospered as a commercial and artistic centre, famously commencing its Gothic cathedral, before internal family rivalries between the Monaldeschi and Filippeschi facilitated direct papal annexation. \n\n Status: Medieval commune of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Orvieto; Common languages: Italian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: Middle Ages; Historical region: Italy

name: Grand Principality of Vladimir
label: russian principalities
description: The Grand Principality of Vladimir was the pre-eminent East Slavic state of north-eastern Rus during the high medieval era, established when Prince Andrey Bogolyubsky relocated the political capital from Suzdal to Vladimir on the Klyazma. Sacking Kiev in 1169, its rulers asserted paramount grand ducal dignity, commissioned monumental white-limestone churches and dominated regional appanages across the Volga-Oka interfluve. The principality's autonomous sovereignty concluded on 4 March 1238 when Grand Prince Yuri II was slain during the devastating Mongol invasion at the Battle of the Sit River. \n\n Status: Sovereign grand principality; Capital: Vladimir; Common languages: Old East Slavic and Church Slavonic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: Grand Prince; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1157; Disestablished: 4 March 1238

name: Inalid Emirate
description: The Inalid Emirate was a Turkoman principality that governed the strategic fortress city of Amid, modern Diyarbakır, and its surrounding Upper Tigris plains. Emerging from the dissolution of Great Seljuk authority, the dynasty successfully navigated complex regional diplomacy by alternating alliances with the Artuqids, the Danismends and the Zangids of Mosul. Their fragile regional autonomy ended on 9 May 1183 when Saladin captured the city following an extended siege and incorporated the domain into the Ayyubid Sultanate. \n\n Status: Sovereign emirate; Capital: Diyarbakır; Common languages: Oghuz Turkic, Arabic and Syriac; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1098; Disestablished: 9 May 1183; Succeeded by: Ayyubid Sultanate

name: Kalachuris of Kalyani
description: The Kalachuris of Kalyani were a prominent Deccan dynasty that seized paramount power across northern Karnataka and Maharashtra by overthrowing the Western Chalukyas in the mid-twelfth century. Governed from the imperial capital of Kalyani under King Bijjala II and his sons, the kingdom witnessed profound socio-religious transformation, including the birth of the Virashaiva Lingayat movement led by the statesman Basavanna and the flourishing of Kannada Vachana poetry. Chalukya loyalists and rival Hoysala forces gradually overwhelmed the state by 1183. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Kalyani; Common languages: Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Jainism, Shaivism and Hinduism; Government: Absolute monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Western Chalukya Empire; Succeeded by: Seuna dynasty and Hoysala Kingdom

name: Khorasani Seljuks
description: The Khorasani Seljuks comprised the eastern successor realm of the Great Seljuk Empire, established in Greater Khorasan following the demise of Sultan Ahmad Sanjar. Centred at the historic oasis metropolis of Merv, the state struggled to preserve imperial authority across eastern Iran, northern Afghanistan and Transoxiana amidst rebellions by nomadic Oghuz tribes. The dynasty maintained courtly Persianate traditions until the rising Khwarazmian Empire and the Ghurids partitioned their eastern territories at the turn of the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Merv; Common languages: Persian, Oghuz Turkic and Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seljuk dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Preceded by: Seljuk Empire; Succeeded by: Khwarazmian Empire and Ghurid dynasty

name: Margraviate of Brandenburg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Margraviate of Brandenburg was an imperial march of the Holy Roman Empire established in the Slavic lands along the Havel and Spree rivers. Founded by Albert the Bear of the House of Ascania following the capture of the fortress of Brenna, the principality spearheaded eastward German settlement through land clearance, town foundations and castle building. Governed from Brandenburg an der Havel, the Ascanians steadily expanded their domain across the Uckermark and Neumark until the extinction of their dynastic line in the early fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Margraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Brandenburg an der Havel; Common languages: Middle Low German and Polabian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: House of Ascania; Ruler title: Margrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1157

name: Mengujekids
description: The Mengujekids were a Turkic dynasty that ruled an autonomous principality in the rugged valleys of northeastern Anatolia, including Erzincan, Kemah and Divriği. Established in the aftermath of the Battle of Manzikert, the dynasty flourished independently following the retreat of imperial Seljuk authority, fostering remarkable architectural innovations culminating in the renowned Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği. The principality retained dynastic autonomy until Sultan Kayqubad I annexed its territories into the Sultanate of Rum in 1228. \n\n Status: Sovereign beylik; Capital: Divriği; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1071; Disestablished: 1228; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Rum

name: Principality of Lutsk
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Lutsk was a medieval East Slavic appanage state established in 1157 upon its partition from the Principality of Volhynia. Situated along the Styr river in western Rus, the principality was governed by a local branch of the Rurikid dynasty from the fortified citadel of Lutsk. The realm played an active role in regional dynastic warfare and trade across Volhynia and Galicia until the early fourteenth century, when it was gradually incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Lutsk; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1157; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Principality of Starodub
label: russian principalities
description: The Principality of Starodub was a medieval Rus appanage principality located in the Severian woodlands along the Babinets river in the Dnieper basin. Formed as a subdivision of the Principality of Chernigov for junior princes of the Olgovichi line, Starodub maintained its own princely court and defensive fortifications to repel nomadic incursions. It preserved local administrative identity through the Mongol suzerainty era until Grand Duke Algirdas incorporated the principality into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Appanage principality; Capital: Starodub; Common languages: Old East Slavic; Religion: Eastern Orthodoxy; Government: Feudal monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Rurik dynasty; Ruler title: Prince; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Grand Duchy of Lithuania

name: Salghurids
description: The Salghurids were a Salur Turkoman dynasty that reigned as the hereditary Atabegs of Fars in southern Iran from their opulent capital at Shiraz. Securing autonomy during the dissolution of the Great Seljuk Empire under Sunqur ibn Mawdud, the dynasty presided over a golden age of Persian literature, urban embellishment and mercantile prosperity along the Persian Gulf. By submitting diplomatically to the Mongol khans, the rulers shielded Fars from devastation until direct Ilkhanate administration was imposed in the late thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign atabegate; Capital: Shiraz; Common languages: Persian and Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Salghurid dynasty; Ruler title: Atabeg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1148; Succeeded by: Ilkhanate

name: Saltukids
description: The Saltukids were an early Anatolian Turkic dynasty centred on the high-altitude fortress city of Erzurum in north-eastern Anatolia. Established following the Seljuk victory at Manzikert, the beylik governed Bayburt, Kars and the upper Araks valley, functioning as a vital defensive march against the expanding Kingdom of Georgia. The principality asserted complete autonomy after the fragmentation of the Great Seljuk Empire until Sultan Suleyman II of Rum deposed the last Saltukid ruler in 1202 to consolidate Anatolia. \n\n Status: Sovereign beylik; Capital: Erzurum; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Bey; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1071; Disestablished: 1202; Succeeded by: Sultanate of Rum

name: Shah-Armens
label: anatolian beyliks
description: The Shah-Armens, also known as the Ahlatshahs, were a Turkoman Muslim dynasty that governed an autonomous realm centred at Ahlat on the north-western shore of Lake Van. Emerging after the Battle of Manzikert, the dynasty exercised sovereign sway over extensive territories across eastern Anatolia and historical Armenia following the collapse of Seljuk authority. Renowned for their imposing monumental tomb towers and thriving lacustrine commerce, the Ahlatshahs retained control of the region until Ayyubid forces conquered their lands in 1207. \n\n Status: Sovereign beylik; Capital: Ahlat; Common languages: Old Anatolian Turkish and Armenian; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: Shah-Armen; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1071; Disestablished: 1207; Succeeded by: Ayyubid dynasty

name: Sultanate of Kerman
description: The Sultanate of Kerman was an autonomous Turco-Persian realm established by a cadet branch of the Seljuk dynasty in south-eastern Iran and Makran. Centred at Kerman, the sultanate commanded strategic overland caravan arteries and flourished through lucrative maritime commerce funnelled through the Persian Gulf ports of Hormuz, Kish and Tiz. The realm maintained political independence and intellectual prestige until devastating dynastic discord enabled nomadic Oghuz invaders under Malik Dinar to overrun the territory in the late twelfth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign sultanate; Capital: Kerman; Common languages: Persian and Oghuz Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Seljuk dynasty; Ruler title: Sultan; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1041; Disestablished: 1187; Succeeded by: Oghuz Turks

name: Zengid Dynasty
description: The Zengid Dynasty was an influential Turkoman dynasty of Atabeg origins that governed Upper Mesopotamia and northern Syria from their principal capital at Mosul. Achieving complete territorial sovereignty following the disintegration of the Great Seljuk Empire, the dynasty spearheaded Muslim counter-offensives against the Crusader states under Imad al-Din Zengi and his son Nur al-Din. Although Saladin subsequently detached their Syrian domains to establish the Ayyubid Sultanate, the Zengid branch at Mosul retained regional governance well into the thirteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign atabegate; Capital: Mosul; Common languages: Arabic, Syriac and Oghuz Turkic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Zengid dynasty; Ruler title: Atabeg; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1127; Succeeded by: Ayyubid dynasty and Luluids

name: Commune of Lodi
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Lodi was a self-governing municipal republic in central Lombardy, founded on 3 August 1158 by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa following the Milanese destruction of ancient Laus Pompeia. Established on the banks of the Adda river, the city guarded essential crossings and developed extensive civic institutions protected by imperial charters. Although frequently contested between imperial loyalty and local autonomy, the commune flourished as a market centre until Visconti expansion incorporated it into the Duchy of Milan in 1335. \n\n Status: Medieval commune of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Lodi; Common languages: Lombard and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 3 August 1158; Disestablished: 1335

name: Burgraviate of Leisnig
label: holy roman empire
description: The Burgraviate of Leisnig was an imperial fief of the Holy Roman Empire established in the Pleissnerland region of Saxony. Anchored at the imposing stronghold of Mildenstein Castle overlooking the Freiberger Mulde, the burgraves held administrative and judicial authority directly under the Hohenstaufen emperors. The territory defended imperial domains against the encroaching Margraves of Meissen, preserving baronial independence until the Wettin dynasty acquired and annexed the estate in 1365. \n\n Status: Burgraviate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Leisnig; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal burgraviate; Ruler title: Burgrave; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1365; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Meissen

name: Lordship of Colditz
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Colditz was an autonomous imperial barony located along the Zwickauer Mulde river in central Saxony. Governed by the noble dynasty of Colditz from their fortified clifftop castle, the lords exercised high justice and managed extensive agricultural lands across the surrounding hills. The barony maintained territorial immediacy under the Holy Roman Crown until financial pressures forced the dynasty to sell the lordship to the Wettin Margraves of Meissen in 1404. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Colditz; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1404; Succeeded by: Margraviate of Meissen

name: Mahdid Dynasty
description: The Mahdid Dynasty was an austere Islamic principality that dominated the coastal Tihama plain and southern highlands of Yemen from their capital at Zabid. Founded by the charismatic religious reformer Ali ibn Mahdi, the movement established a puritanical tribal state that rapidly expanded across southern Arabia by overthrowing the Najahid dynasty. The Mahdid regime maintained stringent ideological rule and continuous warfare against neighbouring principalities until Turan-Shah led an Ayyubid expedition that captured Zabid on 13 May 1174. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Zabid; Common languages: Arabic; Religion: Sunni Islam; Government: Theocratic monarchy; Ruling dynasty: Banu Mahdi; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1159; Disestablished: 13 May 1174; Succeeded by: Ayyubid Sultanate

name: Lordship of Bederkesa
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Bederkesa was a small feudal domain of the Holy Roman Empire located in the marshlands between the lower Weser and Elbe estuaries. Governed by the ministerial knightly family of Bederkesa from their moated castle on Lake Bederkesa, the lordship exercised local judicial and tolls rights over surrounding agrarian parishes. The noble lineage maintained semi-autonomous authority under the Prince-Archbishops of Bremen until chronic debts and local feuds compelled the transfer of the estate to the city of Bremen in the fourteenth century. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Bederkesa; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1382

name: Lordship of Runkel
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Runkel was a baronial territory of the Holy Roman Empire positioned along the lower Lahn river in modern Hesse. Centred on the imposing stone fortress of Runkel Castle, constructed atop a rocky hill to dominate a vital river bridge, the lords of Runkel exercised imperial immediacy and collected river tolls. The lordship engaged in recurrent feuds with the neighbouring House of Nassau and the branch of Runkel-Westerburg, preserving its feudal autonomy until territorial reorganisation in the fifteenth century. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Runkel; Common languages: Middle High German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruling dynasty: House of Runkel; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: Middle Ages

name: Chowta Dynasty
description: The Chowta Dynasty was a matrilineal Jain royal house that ruled the coastal principalities of Tulu Nadu in southwestern Karnataka. Initially established at Puthige and later governing from Moodabidri and the coastal harbour of Ullal, the dynasty patronised magnificent Jain basadis and oversaw active Indian Ocean maritime trade. The state achieved lasting renown under the warrior queen Rani Abbakka Chowta, who repeatedly repulsed Portuguese naval incursions before the kingdom succumbed to regional conquests in the late eighteenth century. \n\n Status: Sovereign principality; Capital: Moodabidri; Common languages: Tulu, Kannada and Sanskrit; Religion: Jainism; Government: Matrilineal monarchy; Ruler title: Raja; Historical era: Middle Ages; Preceded by: Alupa dynasty

name: County of Diepholz
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Diepholz was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire situated in northern Westphalia between the Dümmer Lake and the marshes of the Hunte river. Originating as a noble lordship, the territory gained imperial immediacy and comital rank, allowing the Counts of Diepholz to govern their forested domain with independent territorial laws. The dynasty preserved its distinct sovereignty through diplomatic alignments with neighbouring bishoprics until the extinction of the comital line in 1585 led to its annexation by the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg. \n\n Status: State of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Diepholz; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism and Lutheranism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1585; Succeeded by: Duchy of Brunswick-Luneburg

name: County of Schaunberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The County of Schaunberg was an autonomous noble territory of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Hausruckviertel of Upper Austria along the Danube river. Originating from the lords of Julbach, who received imperial grants at Aschach from Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, the family established their dynastic stronghold at Schaunberg Castle and asserted sovereign comital jurisdiction. The counts fiercely guarded their judicial independence and Danube tolls against the Dukes of Austria until their defeat in the Schaunberg Feud compelled submission to Habsburg overlordship in 1390. \n\n Status: County of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Tholey; Administrative seat: Castle Schaunberg; Common languages: Austro-Bavarian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal county; Ruler title: Count; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Archduchy of Austria

name: Episcopal Lordship of Biella
label: holy roman empire
description: The Episcopal Lordship of Biella was an autonomous ecclesiastical enclave of the Holy Roman Empire situated at the foot of the Biellese Alps in northern Piedmont. Administered by the Bishops of Vercelli, the lordship developed around the fortified upper borough of Piazzo, which received municipal charters, market immunities and judicial rights in the mid-twelfth century. The prince-bishops retained temporal control over local wool manufacturing and alpine valleys until escalating civic unrest prompted the town to submit voluntarily to the House of Savoy in 1379. \n\n Status: Ecclesiastical lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Biella; Common languages: Piedmontese and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical lordship; Ruler title: Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Succeeded by: Duchy of Savoy

name: Landgraviate of Leuchtenberg
label: holy roman empire
description: The Landgraviate of Leuchtenberg was an imperial estate of the Holy Roman Empire located in the Upper Palatinate region of eastern Bavaria. Ruled from the formidable hill fortress of Burg Leuchtenberg, the dynasty exercised imperial immediacy and territorial sovereignty across extensive forests and agricultural lordships near the Bohemian frontier. The landgraves maintained considerable influence in imperial politics, commanding seats in the Imperial Diet until the extinction of the male line in 1646 resulted in the transfer of the domain to the Electorate of Bavaria. \n\n Status: State of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Leuchtenberg; Common languages: Upper German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal landgraviate; Ruler title: Landgrave; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1646; Succeeded by: Electorate of Bavaria

name: Lordship of Windisch-Matrei
label: holy roman empire
description: The Lordship of Windisch-Matrei was an alpine barony of the Holy Roman Empire nestled in the Hohe Tauern mountains of East Tyrol. Established by a branch of the noble Counts of Lechsgemünd, the lordship controlled the strategic valley of the Isel river and guarded mountain approaches across the Felber Tauern pass. The lords governed their isolated highland fief with local judicial authority until 1202, when the dynasty ceded the territory to the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg, converting the district into an episcopal enclave. \n\n Status: Lordship of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Matrei in Osttirol; Common languages: Southern Bavarian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal lordship; Ruler title: Lord; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1202; Succeeded by: Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg

name: Marquisate of Incisa
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Incisa was an independent feudal principality of the Holy Roman Empire situated in the Belbo valley of southern Piedmont. Founded by Alberto del Vasto of the noble House of Aleramici in the twelfth century, the marquisate was administered from the fortified borough of Incisa Scapaccino. Despite its modest territorial extent, the small state staunchly defended its imperial immediacy against the surrounding expansionist states of Montferrat and Savoy until dynastic extinction led to its incorporation into Montferrat in 1548. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Incisa Scapaccino; Common languages: Piedmontese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Aleramici; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Middle Ages; Disestablished: 1548

name: Prince-Bishopric of Schwerin
label: holy roman empire
description: The Prince-Bishopric of Schwerin was an ecclesiastical principality of the Holy Roman Empire established across western Mecklenburg following the twelfth-century Wendish Crusade. Founded by Henry the Lion and consecrated under Bishop Berno, the bishopric exercised secular governance over substantial temporal domains centred on Schwerin Cathedral and surrounding agricultural estates. The prince-bishops maintained their imperial immediacy through centuries of political tension with the Dukes of Mecklenburg until the see was secularised as a duchy under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. \n\n Status: Prince-Bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Schwerin; Common languages: Middle Low German; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Ecclesiastical principality; Ruler title: Prince-Bishop; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1160; Disestablished: 1648; Succeeded by: Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin

name: Republic of Lucca
label: holy roman empire
description: The Republic of Lucca was an independent merchant republic in northwestern Tuscany, emerging as an autonomous city-state from the March of Tuscany in the early 1160s. Enclosed by formidable brick fortifications along the Serchio river, the republic flourished through its world-renowned silk manufacturing, international banking networks and sophisticated oligarchic constitution. Lucca maintained uninterrupted sovereignty and imperial immediacy for over six centuries, skilfully resisting absorption by neighbouring Florence until French revolutionary forces occupied the city on 22 January 1799. \n\n Status: Sovereign republic; Capital: Lucca; Common languages: Italian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Oligarchic republic; Historical era: Middle Ages; Established: 1160; Disestablished: 22 January 1799; Currency: Lucchese ducato

name: Commune of Borgo San Sepolcro
label: holy roman empire
description: The Commune of Borgo San Sepolcro was an autonomous medieval township located in the upper Tiber valley of eastern Tuscany. Established around a tenth-century monastic settlement, the community obtained civic self-government and imperial protection in the mid-twelfth century, constructing robust stone walls and civic palaces. The commune managed vital agricultural and trade routes between Tuscany and Umbria while guarding its republican liberties against regional lords, eventually being absorbed into the signorial realms of Città di Castello and Florence. \n\n Status: Medieval commune of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Sansepolcro; Common languages: Italian and Medieval Latin; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Municipal commune; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Historical region: Italy

name: Kakatiya Dynasty
description: The Kakatiya Dynasty was a major Telugu empire that ruled the eastern Deccan across present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. Throwing off Western Chalukya suzerainty under King Rudradeva in 1163, the dynasty established its fortified capital at Orugallu, modern Warangal, and engineered extensive irrigation reservoirs that transformed agricultural prosperity. Celebrated for the martial reign of Queen Rudrama Devi and its flourishing Telugu literature, the empire maintained sovereignty until sustained sieges by the Delhi Sultanate overwhelmed Prataparudra II in 1323. \n\n Status: Sovereign empire; Capital: Warangal; Common languages: Telugu, Sanskrit and Kannada; Religion: Hinduism and Jainism; Government: Monarchy; Ruler title: King; Historical era: High Middle Ages; Established: 1163; Disestablished: 1323; Succeeded by: Delhi Sultanate and Musunuri Nayakas

name: Marquisate of Romagnano
label: holy roman empire
description: The Marquisate of Romagnano was an imperial fief situated in the Sesia valley and the Po plains of northern Piedmont. Governed by the noble Romagnano di Virle family, who descended from imperial administrators, the marquisate commanded a network of fortified burghs, agricultural communities and river toll stations centred at Romagnano Sesia. The lords exercised territorial jurisdiction and negotiated fragile autonomy between the rising powers of the Duchy of Milan and the House of Savoy before ultimate absorption into the Savoyard state. \n\n Status: Marquisate of the Holy Roman Empire; Capital: Romagnano Sesia; Common languages: Piedmontese and Italian; Religion: Roman Catholicism; Government: Feudal principality; Ruling dynasty: House of Romagnano; Ruler title: Marquis; Historical era: Middle Ages

name: Principality of Orange
label: holy roman empire
